name: Menthol scalp
lead: Menthol scalp refers to using menthol, the cooling compound from mint oils, in scalp serums, tonics, shampoos and conditioners. People use it for the fresh, tingling sensation it gives the scalp, and it appears in hair-care products aimed at a clean, comfortable scalp as the base for healthy-looking hair.[1] Many users also reach for peppermint oil, which contains menthol, in the hope of fuller-looking hair.

Menthol is a monoterpenoid alcohol found in corn mint and peppermint oils. It activates cold-sensitive TRPM8 receptors in the skin, producing a cooling sensation without lowering actual skin temperature, and is used in topical products for itch, minor aches and aftershave.[1]

The hair-growth interest comes from a 2014 mouse study of 3% peppermint oil, which reported faster regrowth than minoxidil in the animals; no controlled human trials of menthol or peppermint oil for hair growth are cited here.[2]

angle.text: Menthol gives scalp products a cooling, refreshing feel and is a common sensory ingredient in tonics and serums. Some people also use peppermint-oil tonics hoping for denser-looking hair, citing a mouse study, alongside the treatments they choose for hair density.

infobox: Mint oils (corn mint, peppermint) or synthetic

paras: In scalp products menthol is chosen mainly for sensation: a cooling tingle on application. The same cooling action is why it features in aftershaves, itch-relief products and sunburn treatments.[1] Wikipedia notes menthol among the ingredients of some natural-style hair conditioners.[1]
Menthol is also used in lip balms, sunburn products, decongestant rubs and as a penetration enhancer for some topical drugs.[1]

Menthol chemically activates TRPM8, the cold-sensing receptor, so skin registers cooling when it is applied. Its analgesic effects are attributed to selective activation of kappa-opioid receptors and reported blockade of calcium and sodium channels.[1]
Menthol carries GHS hazard statements for skin irritation and serious eye irritation, and product labels commonly advise keeping it away from eyes.[1]

Peppermint oil and menthol are not the same material: peppermint oil is a mixture in which menthol is the main compound. A 2014 Toxicological Research paper by Oh, Park and Kim shaved male C57BL/6 mice and applied saline, jojoba oil, 3% minoxidil or 3% peppermint oil in jojoba oil daily for four weeks.[2] The authors reported faster regrowth with peppermint oil from week 2, about 92 percent hair coverage by week 4 against about 55 percent for minoxidil, and more hair follicles than saline or jojoba oil, and proposed that it may promote blood vessel formation around the dermal papilla.[2] The study was in mice and measured only basic safety indicators.[2]
No human studies found on menthol scalp products. The only related research located is the 2014 mouse study of peppermint oil described above.[2]

timeline.event: Oh, Park and Kim report faster hair regrowth in mice treated with 3% peppermint oil than with minoxidil or controls.[2]

card.summary: Cooling mint compound used in scalp serums and tonics for a fresh, soothed-feeling scalp.

quick.overview:
Menthol is the cooling compound from mint oils. In scalp serums, tonics and shampoos it provides a tingling, fresh sensation.

People include it in scalp routines for comfort and the clean feel it gives, alongside whatever they use for hair itself.
quick.mechanism: Menthol activates TRPM8 cold receptors in the skin, so the scalp feels cool without any real temperature change.
quick.risks: Menthol is labelled as a skin and eye irritant. Sensitive scalps can sting, and products are used away from eyes.
